title: The Peach Blossom Fan
subtitle: Borrowing the Joys and Sorrows of Parting and Reunion to Chronicle the Rise and Fall of a Dynasty
description: "The Peach Blossom Fan" is a Qing-dynasty chuanqi play by Kong Shangren. Along with "The Story of the Western Wing," "The Peony Pavilion," and "The Palace of Eternal Youth," it is counted among the Four Great Classical Chinese Dramas. In forty scenes, it traces the love story of Hou Fangyu, a scholar of the Restoration Society, and Li Xiangjun, a famed Qinhuai courtesan, threading through the rise and fall of the Southern Ming Hongguang court—"borrowing the joys and sorrows of parting and reunion to chronicle the rise and fall of a dynasty." It stands as the pinnacle of Chinese historical drama.

route.title: The Peach Blossom Fan: Borrowing the Joys and Sorrows of Parting and Reunion to Chronicle the Rise and Fall of a Dynasty
route.intro:
I watched them raise their vermilion towers, / I watched them feast their guests and friends, / I watched their towers collapse and fall.
Kong Shangren (1648–1718), a native of Qufu, Shandong, was a sixty-fourth-generation descendant of Confucius. In the twenty-third year of the Kangxi reign, during the emperor's southern tour, Kong Shangren was recommended to expound the classics before the throne, earning imperial favor and an official appointment. But his true passion lay not in officialdom but in drama. He traveled extensively to interview Ming loyalists, gather Southern Ming historical records, and spent over a decade completing "The Peach Blossom Fan." When the play premiered, it drew crowds that emptied the streets—but shortly thereafter, Kong Shangren was dismissed from office. "Thin-fated, I suddenly incurred literary enmity; sealing my lips like a bronze figure, I suffered slander." A single drama changed a man's fate. Three centuries later, looking back, that fan upon which blood had been painted into peach blossoms carries not only the joys and sorrows of a talented scholar and a beautiful woman, but also the final breath of a dynasty.

stops.title: Stop One: First Meeting Amid the Misty Waters of Qinhuai
stops.content: In the spring of the sixteenth year of the Chongzhen reign (1643), painted pleasure boats crowded the Qinhuai River in Nanjing, the sounds of strings and bamboo echoing in the distance. Hou Fangyu, a celebrated scholar of the Restoration Society, arrived at the Meixiang Tower of the famed Qinhuai courtesan Li Xiangjun—a small building built by the river, whose windows opened onto the oars and lamplights of the十里 Qinhuai. Hou was twenty-five, in his prime; Li Xiangjun was sixteen, peerless in beauty and talent. Kong Shangren wrote their first meeting as a fan-inscription engagement. Hou Fangyu inscribed a poem on a round fan and presented it to Xiangjun; thus they pledged their troth. The Qinhuai River had witnessed countless romantic dalliances and fleeting liaisons, but only the poem on this fan was real. Along the Qinhuai River in Nanjing, the Zhan Garden lies not far away on Zhanyuan Road. This was the residence garden of Xu Da, Prince of Zhongshan of the Ming dynasty, with Taihu rocks piled into mountains, winding corridors leading to hidden retreats. Emperor Qianlong stayed here during his southern tours and inscribed its name in his own hand. Every rock and stream seems to whisper of the gatherings of late-Ming literati who recited poetry within these walls—Hou Fangyu and his Restoration Society comrades may have discussed the affairs of the realm in just such a garden, fervently believing that the pure stream could wash away the corrupt world.

stops.title: Stop Two: Blood Spatters on the Fan, Peach Blossoms Bloom
stops.content: Tragedy struck at the most beautiful moment. Ruan Dacheng, the treacherous official who had thrown in his lot with the eunuch faction, sought to win over the Restoration Society through Hou Fangyu. He sent Xiangjun a dowry: gold and silver jewelry, brocade and silk garments, chest after chest carried into Meixiang Tower. Xiangjun was too clever to be fooled—she knew at once that the source of these riches was unclean. She pressed Hou for the truth, and upon learning it was from Ruan Dacheng, flew into a rage. Before the assembled company, she pulled the hairpins from her head and hurled back every piece of jewelry, weeping as she spoke: "Unthinking, you speak so lightly. To dispel his calamities for him, to scheme for him—that takes no small effort!" Rather live in honorable poverty than stain her integrity by even a hair. This was the celebrated "Rejecting the Dowry"—a sixteen-year-old girl from the pleasure quarters showed all the world that integrity does not depend on social standing, and righteousness does not care about wealth or poverty. The Qinhuai River has flowed for a thousand years, witnessing countless romantic affairs, but such unbending moral backbone belongs to this one woman alone. Later, Hou Fangyu was forced to flee Nanjing. The eunuch faction remnant Tian Yang, coveting Xiangjun's beauty, tried to force her into marriage. Xiangjun would rather die than submit. She slammed her head against the dressing table, and her blood splattered onto the fan inscribed with the love poem. Her friend Yang Longyou, who had come to visit, was distraught at the sight. Then a sudden inspiration struck—he picked up a brush, and following the contours of the bloodstains on the fan, he sketched a few branches, the blood drops transforming into peach blossoms in full bloom. From that day on, the fan acquired a name both tragic and immortal—the Peach Blossom Fan. These were no ordinary peach blossoms—they were flowers watered with a person's very life. "Splashed blood turned into peach blossoms on the fan, more vivid than any growing on the branch." Kong Shangren's lyric is masterful: peach blossoms growing on a branch are merely ordinary spring scenery, but the blood-peach on the fan is a heart that refuses to bow. Today, walking through Nanjing, the beaded curtains and painted boats along the Qinhuai River are no longer as they were in the late Ming, but the spirit lingers. Visit the Zhan Garden—in this Ming-dynasty garden of the residence of Xu Da, Prince of Zhongshan, the Taihu rockeries are exquisitely translucent, and through the winding corridors, you can faintly hear the rustle of wind through bamboo leaves. Long ago, Hou Fangyu and his Restoration Society comrades passionately debated the great affairs of the realm in just such a garden—the eunuch faction in power, the country in peril, who could save the Ming empire? Little did they dream that in Meixiang Tower by the Qinhuai River, a sixteen-year-old girl, with her fiery blood, answered that question more powerfully than any of their essays. Then climb the Nanjing City Wall—the longest ancient city wall in the world, winding for thirty-three kilometers, its bricks fired by a million craftsmen under Zhu Yuanzhang over six hundred years ago, still as hard as iron. The clear inscriptions on those bricks, like the blood-stained peach blossom on the fan, are the most solemn signatures that ordinary people have left to history. Standing on the wall and looking down, the Qinhuai River runs like a silver ribbon through the ancient city—on its surface is reflected the shadow of Li Xiangjun, who would never bow her head.

stops.title: Stop Three: The Kingly Spirit of Jinling Fades in Shadow
stops.content: On the nineteenth day of the third month of the seventeenth year of the Chongzhen reign (1644), Li Zicheng captured Beijing, and the Chongzhen Emperor hanged himself on Coal Hill. When the news reached Nanjing, the entire city dressed in mourning; cries shook the heavens—the Ming dynasty, though battered, had endured for 276 years, and now it was truly dead. Ma Shiying, Ruan Dacheng, and their faction installed Prince Fu, Zhu Yousong, as emperor in Nanjing—the Southern Ming Hongguang court was hastily established. Yet this small court, from top to bottom, lived in drunken revelry: "National enmity can be forgiven, but private grudges are hardest to resolve." Ruan Dacheng busied himself compiling the "List of Locusts and Grubs" to take revenge on the Donglin and Restoration Societies; Ma Shiying hurried to plunder the people's wealth; Prince Fu busied himself selecting beauties and rehearsing new plays. The Hongguang Emperor even hung a couplet in his palace: "Nothing matters more than a cup in hand; in a hundred years, how often does one see the moon overhead?" The nation was on the verge of extinction, yet he still drowned himself in drunken pleasure. Amid such absurdity, the Qing army swept southward, irresistible. The Ten Days of Yangzhou, the Three屠s of Jiading—each piece of news struck Nanjing like a thunderbolt. The painted boats on the Qinhuai River fell silent, one by one. Xiangjun and Hou Fangyu were separated, each stranded in a different place—one in hiding, the other forcibly conscripted into the palace. The Qinhuai River, once dyed with rouge, was about to be scorched to ash by the fires of war. Today, standing on the Sacred Way of the Ming Xiaoling Mausoleum, the achievements of Zhu Yuanzhang six hundred years ago have been frozen in the silence of the stone statues. Those stone horses, elephants, and camels—how many dynastic changes, how many joys and sorrows have they witnessed? Climb the Nanjing City Wall to look over the ancient city—this is the Nanjing where Hou Fangyu and Li Xiangjun lived. The names of the craftsmen who built the wall are engraved on the bricks, like the blood-stained peach blossom on the fan—the most solemn signatures ordinary people leave to history.

stops.title: Stop Four: Entering the Way Amid White Clouds at Qixia Mountain
stops.content: In the second year of the Shunzhi reign (1645), the Qing army breached Yangzhou. Shi Kefa died for his country; soon, Nanjing fell. The Hongguang Emperor was captured; the Southern Ming was extinguished. Hou Fangyu and Li Xiangjun each fled for their lives through the chaos, until finally, by an unexpected twist of fate, they encountered each other at the White Cloud Nunnery on Qixia Mountain outside Nanjing. Two people who had suffered the pain of national subjugation and the bitterness of separation now held each other's hands and gazed—they were no longer the talented scholar and beautiful woman of years past. Hou Fangyu wanted to go into seclusion with Xiangjun and live out their remaining days together. But an old Daoist in the nunnery thundered: "Where is the nation? Where is your home? Where is your sovereign? Where is your father? Is this fleeting bond of romance the only thing you cannot cut through?" The words struck them like a thunderbolt—the mountains and rivers were shattered, the people scattered. In the face of such devastating loss, what were their personal loves and passions? Hou Fangyu and Li Xiangjun stood facing each other in silence, then each entered monastic life in sorrow. Kong Shangren ended his protagonists' story in the cruelest possible way. On the mountain where the White Cloud Nunnery stood, there is an ancient monastery—the Qixia Temple Relic Pagoda. This Southern Tang stone pagoda is carved with exquisite craftsmanship; a thousand years of wind and frost have not worn away the features of a single Buddha on its surface. It stands in silent witness, having seen Emperor Wu of Liang worship Buddha, having witnessed the rise and fall of Jinling through the ages, and having heard the bitter question Kong Shangren placed in the mouth of the old Daoist.

stops.title: Stop Five: The Ten Days of Yangzhou—Loyal Souls Remain
stops.content: "The Peach Blossom Fan" contains a passage that is almost unbearable to read—Shi Kefa's desperate defense of Yangzhou. The Qing army was at the gates; the city had few troops and fewer generals. Shi Kefa knew he could not hold out, yet he was determined to "bend every effort to serve the nation unto death." With three thousand shattered soldiers, he faced hundreds of thousands of Qing troops. On the day the city fell, he slit his own throat and died for his country. Kong Shangren wrote his dying lament: "Fight together to defend the city; die to repay the nation." Just eight words, but they captured the entire essence of a loyal minister in a dying age. After his death, the people of Yangzhou could not find his body, so they built a cenotaph at the foot of Plum Blossom Hill—within it were buried his robe, belt, and official tablet. Shi Kefa's cenotaph lies at the foot of Plum Blossom Hill in Yangzhou. And after the Qing army breached the city, Yangzhou suffered the horrific "Ten Days of Yangzhou"—massacring 800,000 people, the river waters turning red. Wang Xiuchu, in his "Account of the Ten Days of Yangzhou," recorded: "The corpses in the city piled up like tangled hemp; blood flowed in channels from the West Gate to the East Gate, along every street." The mere mention of that catastrophe still tightens the heart of every Yangzhou native. 800,000 lives bought the Qing army's deterrence in the Jiangnan region—from that day forward, the Southern Ming resistance lost all will to fight. Today, Yangzhou is a city of prosperity. The Ge Garden's four-season rockeries delight with their artistry—spring hills of bamboo and stone, summer hills of clouds and water, autumn hills of red leaves, winter hills of white snow. The people of Yangzhou have packed all four seasons into a single garden. Through a few alleys, the He Garden's double-level winding corridors twist and turn, earning it the title "Finest Garden of the Late Qing." Strolling through these exquisitely refined gardens, visitors may find it hard to imagine that 370 years ago, on this very same land, the people of Yangzhou, with the most tragic sacrifice, showed the world what it means that "everyone is responsible for the rise or fall of the nation." Shi Kefa's cenotaph still lies at the foot of Plum Blossom Hill. The tombstone reads: "Tomb of Shi Kefa, Imperial Commissioner of the Ming, Minister of War and Grand Secretary of the Eastern Pavilion." At Qingming Festival, the people of Yangzhou quietly place a spray of plum blossoms before his tomb. The blood-stained peach blossom on the fan is the flower of Hou Fangyu and Li Xiangjun's love, but also the eternal mark of the patriotic sentiment of all the Chinese people.

stops.title: Stop Six: Epilogue—Sending Off the Southern Dynasty Beneath the Peach Blossom Fan
stops.content: Kong Shangren finished "The Peach Blossom Fan," and the entire play ends abruptly with that thunderous shout on Qixia Mountain—"Where is the nation? Where is your home? Where is your sovereign? Where is your father?" But the story did not truly end. The historical Hou Fangyu, in the eighth year of the Shunzhi reign (1651), sat for the Qing imperial examination and passed in the secondary list. The once-fervent scholar of the Restoration Society had finally bowed to reality. It is said that when Li Xiangjun learned of this, she was overcome with grief and rage, vomiting blood and dying. No one knows where she was buried—perhaps her ashes were scattered into the Qinhuai River, the river where she was born and where she died. Kong Shangren's fate was even more dramatic. After "The Peach Blossom Fan" premiered in the thirty-eighth year of the Kangxi reign (1699), it took the capital by storm. Even the Kangxi Emperor himself sent someone to request a copy. But Kong Shangren was soon dismissed from office. Some say the play's veiled descriptions of Qing army atrocities angered the court; others say he was caught up in a literary inquisition. He returned to his hometown of Qufu after his dismissal and died in obscurity and sorrow. A single drama changed a dynasty's literary climate and a man's fate. Today, when you enter the Chaotian Palace in Nanjing—the Ming-dynasty ritual hall for audiences with the Son of Heaven, later converted into the Jiangning Prefecture Confucian School in the Qing dynasty, now the Nanjing Municipal Museum—you will see yellowed playbills, faded costumes, and replicas of the Peach Blossom Fan. The drama may have long since ended, but history continues. The stone steps before Chaotian Palace's Lingxing Gate have been polished smooth by the feet of countless visitors, bearing layer upon layer the imprints of Ming scholar-officials' court boots, Qing scholars' cloth shoes, Republic-era students' leather shoes, and today's sneakers. Each generation that enters here seeks its own answers. "I watched them raise their vermilion towers, / I watched them feast their guests and friends, / I watched their towers collapse and fall." —And after the towers fell? On the ruins, new towers are built, and new towers too grow old. This is Nanjing, this is China—a civilization forever cycling through destruction and rebirth. The blood-colored peach blossom on the fan bloomed in an age of national ruin, but its seed was planted in the hearts of all Chinese people.
